findings.recommendation: Use stage_privately. Create the staging area with tempfile.mkdtemp (mode 0700, unpredictable name) and the file with tempfile.mkstemp inside it; never stage under a fixed, world-writable path.

findings.title: Rate limiter keyed by RemoteAddr including the ephemeral port, and never refilled
findings.evidence: Throttle keys the limiter on r.RemoteAddr (gateway-limits/middleware/limits.go:20). In net/http RemoteAddr is the connection's "IP:port", where the port is the client's ephemeral source port and differs for every new TCP connection. Two consequences follow from that single choice. First, an attacker gets a fresh full bucket per connection simply by not reusing the keep-alive connection, so the limit never engages. Second, `buckets` accumulates one permanent entry per connection -- allow() at lines 29-37 only ever inserts and decrements, there is no eviction and no TTL, so the map grows without bound. Separately, the bucket is a plain counter that is only ever decremented (line 36): there is no refill, so a legitimate client that reuses one connection is denied permanently after `burst` requests rather than for a window.  Related locations: gateway-limits/middleware/limits.go:36.
findings.impact: The control fails in both directions at once. An attacker bypasses it entirely by opening new connections, while doing so grows a process-lifetime map until the gateway exhausts memory -- so the bypass is itself the denial of service. A well-behaved keep-alive client, meanwhile, is locked out for the process's lifetime after its first burst.
findings.recommendation: Key on the client IP only (net.SplitHostPort, or the validated forwarded-for header behind a trusted proxy), and use a token bucket that refills over time with bounded, expiring per-key state.

findings.title: Rate-limiting middleware is defined but wired to no route
findings.evidence: middleware.Throttle (gateway-limits/middleware/limits.go:18-26) is exported, complete, and reads its burst from config.RateLimitBurst, which config.Load() populates (config/env.go:35). It appears nowhere in router/routes.go: the mux built at lines 12-19 wraps two routes in BodyLimit and none in Throttle. The entire public, session-less surface -- including the upload path and the signature-verifying delivery webhook -- is served with no request-rate control of any kind.  Related locations: gateway-limits/middleware/limits.go:18.
findings.impact: Unlimited request volume against unauthenticated endpoints: brute-forcing the X-Signature value on /v1/hooks/delivery, unbounded storage writes and cost via /v1/upload, and straightforward resource exhaustion. The configured RATE_LIMIT_BURST knob gives operators a false assurance that a limit is in force.
findings.recommendation: Compose the middlewares on the mux -- Throttle(BodyLimit(mux)) -- so every route inherits both, rather than opting each route in by hand.

findings.title: Missing ReadTimeout and IdleTimeout on the HTTP server
findings.evidence: gateway-limits/server.go:14-19 configures ReadHeaderTimeout and WriteTimeout from config.StreamTimeout but leaves ReadTimeout and IdleTimeout at their zero values, which in net/http means no limit. ReadHeaderTimeout bounds only the header phase, so a client that sends valid headers and then dribbles the body holds the connection and its goroutine. IdleTimeout is worse than it looks: net/http falls back to ReadTimeout when IdleTimeout is zero, and ReadTimeout is also zero here, so keep-alive connections are never reaped at all. config.StreamTimeout itself defaults to 300 (config/env.go:36), so even the timeouts that are set are five minutes long.
findings.impact: Slow-body and idle keep-alive connections accumulate until the process runs out of file descriptors and goroutines, denying service to legitimate callers. This compounds with the unbounded io.ReadAll on /v1/upload: a slow, large body occupies both memory and a connection slot for as long as the attacker cares to hold it.
findings.recommendation: Set ReadTimeout and IdleTimeout explicitly, keep them short relative to the header timeout, and do not reuse a single 300-second knob for every phase.

findings.title: Container image runs the application as root on a development server
findings.evidence: intake-portal/Dockerfile has no USER directive anywhere in its seven lines, so the CMD at line 7 executes as uid 0. That CMD is `flask run --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000` -- the Werkzeug development server, which is single-threaded, has no hardening, and is explicitly documented by Flask as unsuitable for production. docker-compose.yml builds this same image and publishes it on 0.0.0.0:8000 (lines 2-9), so this is the shipped runtime, not a local convenience.
findings.impact: Any code-execution flaw in the application -- and this service has several reachable ones -- lands as root inside the container, removing the last barrier before a container escape or a write to any mounted volume. The development server additionally exposes the interactive debugger if FLASK_DEBUG is ever set in this environment, which is direct remote code execution.
findings.recommendation: Create an unprivileged user and add USER before CMD, and serve with a production WSGI server (gunicorn or uwsgi) rather than `flask run`.

findings.title: Log injection through unsanitized concatenation in record_rejection
findings.evidence: record_rejection at intake-portal/app/audit.py:13-14 builds its message by string concatenation: `logger.info("submission " + form_id + " rejected: " + reason)`. Both interpolated values originate from the request. The two neighbouring functions in the same file are both safe and show the author knew the alternatives: record_submission (line 9) uses lazy %s arguments, and record_export (line 17) emits json.dumps. Concatenation also defeats the logging module's own argument handling, so any formatting directive that survives into the message is interpreted as a format string by downstream handlers.  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: record_submission (audit.py:9) and record_export (audit.py:17).
findings.impact: An attacker embeds newlines and a well-formed fake log line in `reason` to forge audit entries -- for example a fabricated 'submission X accepted for admin' -- which corrupts the audit trail that this module exists to provide and can mislead an incident investigation. Injected control characters and format directives can also break or poison downstream log parsers and SIEM ingestion.
findings.recommendation: Use lazy formatting as record_submission does -- logger.info("submission %s rejected: %s", form_id, reason) -- or emit structured JSON as record_export does, and strip or escape newline characters in attacker-controlled values.

findings.title: Retention check compares a timestamp against itself and can never expire a record
findings.evidence: intake-portal/app/store.py:17-18 -- `return isoparse(created_at) + timedelta(days=RETENTION_DAYS) < isoparse(created_at)`. Both sides derive from the same created_at value, so the expression reduces to `t + 90 days < t`. For any positive RETENTION_DAYS -- the default is 90 (settings.py:9) -- this is false for every input, on every date, forever. The right-hand side was evidently meant to be the current time. The function has no other caller-visible effect, so nothing else compensates.
findings.impact: The retention policy is inoperative. No record is ever classified as expired, so nothing is ever deleted and personal data submitted through the intake portal is retained indefinitely, in direct contradiction of the configured RETENTION_DAYS. The failure is silent and would pass any test that only asserts fresh records are not expired.
findings.recommendation: Compare against the current time: `isoparse(created_at) + timedelta(days=RETENTION_DAYS) < datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. Add a test that pins a created_at older than the window and asserts True.

findings.title: No cumulative element budget across nested maps and lists
findings.evidence: readMap (wire-decoder/src/ValueDecoder.java:38-45) and readList (lines 47-54) each read a 16-bit entry count -- up to 65,535 -- and loop that many times allocating objects, with no budget shared between them and no ceiling on the total number of elements produced by one frame. This is a distinct defect from the recursion depth: even at a modest depth of two or three, the counts multiply, so a container declaring 65,535 entries whose values are themselves containers describes an object graph orders of magnitude larger than the bytes that described it. Settings has no constant for a total element or object budget. The amplification is unconstrained here specifically because ValueDecoder reads a raw DataInputStream (line 12) rather than the bounded body array that FrameReader.readFrame produces, so a peer is not even limited to MAX_FRAME_BYTES of description.  Related locations: wire-decoder/src/ValueDecoder.java:49.
findings.impact: Heap exhaustion from a compact input -- HashMap and ArrayList entries, plus the boxed values and String keys behind them, consume far more memory than the wire bytes that requested them. The result is OutOfMemoryError or sustained GC thrashing that denies service without any single allocation looking unreasonable, so it evades a per-allocation size check of the kind readText applies.
findings.recommendation: Carry a mutable remaining-element and remaining-byte budget through the decode of a single frame, decrementing it for every element and every allocated byte, and abort with MalformedFrameException when it is exhausted. Bound each container's entry count against the bytes actually remaining in the frame rather than against the width of the count field.

findings.title: Floating dependency ranges and an abandoned dependency in a package that executes install hooks
findings.evidence: node-supply/package.json pins some dependencies exactly (node-fetch 2.7.0, typescript 5.4.5) but leaves three on caret ranges: chalk ^5.3.0 (line 13), @acme/internal-config ^1.0.0 (line 15) and left-pad ^1.3.0 (line 17). A caret range resolves at install time, so without a committed lockfile every install may pull code that has never been reviewed here. left-pad is additionally a one-function package that is famous precisely as a supply-chain cautionary tale and is not imported anywhere in this tree. The risk is elevated specifically because this manifest declares a preinstall hook (line 8) and is published (line 4), so the package sits upstream of other people's builds.  Related locations: node-supply/package.json:17.  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: node-fetch and typescript, which are pinned exactly in the same manifest.
findings.impact: A compromised or maliciously republished minor version of any floating dependency is installed automatically, without a code change here and without review, and executes on every developer and CI machine that installs this package or anything depending on it.
findings.recommendation: Pin exact versions, commit a lockfile and install with `npm ci`; remove unused dependencies such as left-pad; and enable npm's audit/provenance signals in CI.

findings.title: Internal-scope dependency resolvable from the public registry by consumers
findings.evidence: node-supply/package.json:15 depends on `"@acme/internal-config": "^1.0.0"`, a package in the organization's private @acme scope. The repository's .npmrc maps that scope to the internal registry (`@acme:registry=https://npm.internal.acme.example/`), which resolves it correctly for anyone building inside this checkout. But .npmrc is repository-local configuration and is not published with the package, while package.json:5 sets `"private": false` -- this package is published to the public registry. A consumer who installs @acme/billing-cli inherits the dependency without inheriting the scope mapping, so their npm resolves @acme/internal-config against registry.npmjs.org.  Related locations: node-supply/.npmrc:2.
findings.impact: An attacker publishes @acme/internal-config to the public npm registry at a version satisfying ^1.0.0. Every downstream consumer of this CLI -- and any internal build whose .npmrc is missing or overridden -- installs the attacker's package instead of the internal one, giving code execution in their build. This is the classic dependency-confusion path, and it is opened specifically by publishing a package that depends on a private-scope name.
findings.recommendation: Do not ship a public package that depends on a private-scope name: vendor the configuration, inline it, or publish @acme/internal-config publicly as a defensive placeholder owned by the organization. Additionally register the scope name on the public registry so it cannot be claimed.

findings.title: Account deletion never reaches four of the five declared stores
findings.evidence: The module declares its own scope at analytics-service/jobs/lifecycle.py:5: STORES = ("customers", "events", "exports", "search_index", "backups"). delete_account (line 8) issues a single statement that soft-deletes only the customers row. purge_expired (line 13) does iterate all five stores, but its predicate is `WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL AND deleted_at < %s` -- and nothing ever sets deleted_at on rows in events, exports, search_index or backups. The two functions therefore combine into a deletion pipeline that can never remove data from four of the five stores the module itself names.  Related locations: analytics-service/jobs/lifecycle.py:5.
findings.impact: A customer who exercises a deletion right has their record flagged, while their event history, generated exports, search index entries and backups are retained indefinitely and remain queryable. This is a silent failure of a compliance control -- the system reports the deletion as successful.
findings.recommendation: Have delete_account mark, or enqueue deletion for, every store in STORES -- iterate the same tuple purge_expired iterates -- so that the declared scope and the executed scope cannot drift apart.

findings.title: Third-party tracking tags rendered with no consent gate
findings.evidence: load_trackers at analytics-service/jobs/lifecycle.py:20-25 unconditionally returns two third-party script tags -- cdn.metrics.example and ads.partner.example -- for any page. Neither the visitor's consent state nor any category preference is consulted; the `page` argument is not even read. The sibling load_trackers_after_consent (line 28) takes a consent dict, returns an empty list when the analytics category was not accepted, and drops the advertising vendor entirely.  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: load_trackers_after_consent (lifecycle.py:28).
findings.impact: Every visitor's browsing is disclosed to an analytics vendor and an advertising vendor before any consent is collected, and the ad vendor is loaded even for visitors who accept only analytics. Loading a third-party script also grants that vendor arbitrary script execution in the site's origin.
findings.recommendation: Use load_trackers_after_consent and gate each vendor on its own consent category; do not emit any third-party tag before a consent decision exists.

findings.title: Untrusted ticket bodies indexed for retrieval with no provenance metadata
findings.evidence: ingest_ticket at rag-agent/agent/memory.py:26-28 calls index.add_texts([ticket['body']]) with no metadatas argument. The ticket body is written by a customer, and once it is in the index it is indistinguishable from curated internal documentation at retrieval time -- there is nothing for a retriever or a prompt builder to filter on. The sibling ingest_ticket_marked (line 31) passes metadatas=[{'origin': 'customer-ticket', 'trust': 'untrusted', 'ticket_id': ...}], and its docstring states that retrieval filters on exactly those fields. build_prompt_marked in answer.py consumes d['origin'] and d['trust'], so the downstream consumer of this metadata already exists -- unmarked documents simply cannot be labelled by it.  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: ingest_ticket_marked (memory.py:31).
findings.impact: This is the write half of the indirect prompt injection path: it is what lets attacker-authored text enter the corpus that build_prompt later splices into the model context, and it removes the one signal that would have allowed the safe prompt builder to mark that text as untrusted.
findings.recommendation: Use ingest_ticket_marked so every indexed chunk carries origin and trust, and have the retriever and prompt builder consume those fields -- rejecting or clearly demarcating untrusted content.

findings.title: Unverified vendored linter executed inside the credentialed publish stage
findings.evidence: pipelines-migration/scripts/thirdparty-lint.sh:4 runs `exec node ./vendor/lint-bundle/cli.js --config .lintrc.json`, and the comment on line 3 states the bundle is 'Vendored from the upstream linter project; refreshed by hand every few months'. There is no pinned version, no checksum, and no provenance record for the vendored bytes -- a manual refresh is an unreviewed code drop. The Jenkinsfile invokes this script at line 21, inside the withCredentials block that binds NPM_TOKEN (line 19), and between `npm ci` and `npm publish`.  Related locations: pipelines-migration/Jenkinsfile:21.
findings.impact: Whatever ends up in vendor/lint-bundle executes with the npm publish token in its environment, immediately before the publish step. A tampered or compromised upstream bundle -- or a careless manual refresh -- exfiltrates the token or modifies the build output between lint and publish, yielding a poisoned released package.
findings.recommendation: Install the linter as a pinned, integrity-checked dependency rather than a hand-refreshed vendored bundle, and record a checksum for the vendored bytes if vendoring is retained. Move linting out of the withCredentials block so no lint-time code sees the publish token.

findings.title: National ID and email written to application logs in log_request
findings.evidence: log_request at analytics-service/app/logging_setup.py:11-12 emits `user["email"]` and `user["national_id"]` as ordinary log fields on every request. Logs are the highest-fanout data sink in a service: they are shipped to aggregators, retained far longer than the records themselves, and are readable by operators and support staff who have no need for identity documents. RedactingFormatter at line 20 does match this format and would scrub the fields, but nothing in the tree attaches that formatter to a handler, so the redaction is unattached defence-in-depth rather than an active control, and it cannot protect any sink that receives the record before formatting (structured/JSON handlers receive record.args intact).  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: log_request_redacted (logging_setup.py:15).
findings.impact: Identity documents and email addresses accumulate in log storage and log-aggregation vendors with a wider audience and longer retention than the customer record itself; compromise or over-broad access to logging infrastructure yields a full PII corpus.
findings.recommendation: Use log_request_redacted, which logs only the opaque user id. If a formatter-based control is retained, attach RedactingFormatter to every handler explicitly and do not rely on it for structured handlers that serialize record.args directly.

findings.title: Boolean configuration flag stored as a string, so the flag never means what it says
findings.evidence: intake-portal/app/settings.py:7 -- VERIFY_WEBHOOK_AUDIENCE = os.environ.get("VERIFY_WEBHOOK_AUDIENCE", "false"). The value is a str, never coerced. In Python the string "false" is truthy, so any consumer written as `if VERIFY_WEBHOOK_AUDIENCE:` takes the enabled branch both for the default and for an operator who explicitly sets the variable to false -- while a consumer written as `if VERIFY_WEBHOOK_AUDIENCE == "true":` takes the disabled branch even when an operator sets it to True, 1 or yes. The sibling lines 8 and 9 show the author's own correct pattern -- EXPORT_PAGE_SIZE and RETENTION_DAYS are wrapped in int(). No consumer of this flag exists in the tree, so the direction of the failure cannot be established here; what is established is that the flag's value cannot be relied upon by either idiom.  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: EXPORT_PAGE_SIZE / RETENTION_DAYS, which are coerced with int() (settings.py:8-9).
findings.impact: A security control whose on/off state is decided by a string-truthiness accident rather than by the operator. Whichever idiom the consuming code uses, one of the two configurations silently does the opposite of what the operator asked, and the name (verify webhook audience) indicates the control gates an authentication property.
findings.recommendation: Parse it explicitly -- e.g. os.environ.get(...,"false").strip().lower() in {"1","true","yes"} -- and default a verification flag to enabled, matching the int() coercion already used on the two settings below it.

findings.title: readLabel allocates from a peer-declared length without consulting the declared limit
findings.evidence: readLabel at wire-decoder/src/FrameReader.java:24-29 reads an unsigned short length (line 25) and immediately allocates new byte[length] (line 26) followed by a blocking readFully. It never compares the value against Settings.MAX_STRING_BYTES, even though Settings exists precisely to hold 'limits the peer cannot change' and readLabel's own sibling in this class -- readFrame, directly above at lines 14-22 -- does check its length against Settings.MAX_FRAME_BYTES and throws MalformedFrameException. The parallel method in the other class, ValueDecoder.readText, likewise checks MAX_STRING_BYTES. Today the 16-bit field width caps the allocation at 65,536 bytes, which coincidentally equals MAX_STRING_BYTES + 1, so the practical bound holds by accident of the type rather than by any check in the code.  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: FrameReader.readFrame (FrameReader.java:14) and ValueDecoder.readText.
findings.impact: A peer forces a 64 KiB allocation and a blocking readFully per label with no frame-level accounting, which contributes to the amplification described for readMap and readList. More importantly the safety property is undeclared: it rests on the width of the length field, so any change to a 32-bit length -- the exact shape ValueDecoder.readBlob already has -- silently removes the bound with no code change at this call site.
findings.recommendation: Check length against Settings.MAX_STRING_BYTES and throw MalformedFrameException when it is exceeded, matching readFrame directly above and ValueDecoder.readText, so the bound is stated rather than inferred from the field width.

findings.title: Action referenced by a mutable tag in the privileged workflow
findings.evidence: terraform-platform/.github/workflows/deploy.yml:13 uses `actions/checkout@v4`. A tag is a mutable pointer: whatever commit v4 designates at run time is what executes. In this workflow that code runs in a pull_request_target context holding a write-all token and repository secrets, which is the highest-value possible context. The same repository already applies the stricter convention where it matters to the author: release.yml:18 pins the identical action to a full commit SHA with the version recorded in a trailing comment (`actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2`).  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: release.yml:18, which SHA-pins the same action.
findings.impact: If the tag is repointed -- by a compromise of the action's repository or of a maintainer account -- the new code runs automatically in the privileged job with no change here and no review. The exposure is bounded by the trustworthiness of a third party rather than by anything this repository controls.
findings.recommendation: Pin every action to a full commit SHA with the human-readable version in a comment, as release.yml does, and keep them current with an automated updater.

findings.title: Hardcoded database password committed in docker-compose.yml
findings.evidence: intake-portal/docker-compose.yml:14 sets POSTGRES_PASSWORD: intake as a literal, and line 5 wires the application to it with DATABASE_URL: postgresql://db/intake. The password equals the database name and the service name, so it is guessable even without reading the file. Unlike .env.example -- which is a template and whose placeholders are legitimate -- a compose file is executable configuration: this value is the password the database is actually created with wherever this file is used.  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: the .env.example placeholders, which are correctly non-functional templates.
findings.impact: Anyone who reaches the database port, including a neighbouring container on the default compose network or an attacker who has achieved any code execution in the environment, authenticates with a password published in the repository and reads or modifies the full intake data set. Committed credentials also outlive the environment: they persist in history and are routinely reused into staging and production.
findings.recommendation: Reference an environment variable or a secret (POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?required}) supplied from a .env file that is git-ignored or from the platform's secret store, and generate a distinct value per environment.

findings.title: Unscoped aggregate statistics exposed to every authenticated user
findings.evidence: certs-authz/api/resources.py:39-40 -- CertificatesStats.get calls service.counts_by_month() with no argument. The sibling read endpoint in the same file, CertificatesList.get (line 15), passes service.current_user() so the listing is scoped to the caller. The stats endpoint drops that argument, and AuthenticatedResource supplies only a session, not a role.  Hardened counterpart present in the tree: CertificatesList.get (resources.py:14).
findings.impact: Any authenticated user, including one with no authority roles, learns the system-wide certificate issuance volume broken down by month. In a multi-tenant certificate service that discloses other tenants' infrastructure growth and deployment cadence, and gives an attacker a reliable oracle for whether a targeted issuance occurred.
findings.recommendation: Scope the aggregate to the caller's authorities, as CertificatesList.get does, or require an operator role for the global view.

findings.title: Unencoded partner id interpolated into an internal service URL path
findings.evidence: partner_name at intake-portal/app/tokens.py:15-16 builds its request as `requests.get(f"{DIRECTORY}/{partner_id}", timeout=5)`, where DIRECTORY is the fixed internal endpoint https://partners.internal/v1/directory (line 8). partner_id is interpolated with no URL-encoding and no format validation. requests forwards the path substantially as given, so characters that are structural in a URL -- ../, ?, #, and an encoded scheme separator -- change which resource, and in some cases which endpoint, is addressed on an internal host that trusts the caller's network position.
findings.impact: A partner id containing traversal or query characters redirects the lookup to a different path on the internal directory service, reaching internal endpoints that were never intended to be caller-selectable, and the response is returned into the application. The blast radius depends on the directory service, which is outside this tree, so this is reported as a latent injection rather than a proven bypass.
findings.recommendation: Validate partner_id against its expected shape (a UUID or a bounded alphanumeric id) before use, and pass it through urllib.parse.quote with an empty safe set rather than interpolating it into the path.

findings.title: Publish job triggers on any tag while only v* tags are protected
findings.evidence: pipelines-migration/.gitlab-ci.yml:46-52 gates the publish stage on `if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG'` (line 49) -- which matches every tag, of any shape. docs/ci-settings-export.md:18 records that the protected tag pattern is `v*`. The two do not line up: pushing a tag that does not match v* starts the publish job on an unprotected ref. NPM_PUBLISH_TOKEN is Protected (export line 13), so it is withheld on an unprotected ref and the npm publish call fails -- the immediate failure mode is closed, not open. What remains is a real policy gap: the job's own trigger condition does not encode the protection rule it depends on, so the safety of this stage rests entirely on a setting held in another system.
findings.impact: Any developer who can push a tag can start the credentialed publish job on an unprotected ref. Today it fails for want of the token, but the pipeline is one settings change -- unprotecting the variable, or widening the protected-tag pattern -- away from allowing an unreviewed publish, and the misalignment is invisible from the repository alone. It also produces noisy failed publish jobs that train reviewers to ignore them.
findings.recommendation: Make the trigger match the protection rule: `if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v/'`, so the job's condition and the protected-tag pattern are stated in the same place and cannot drift apart.

findings.title: clean() ignores its target and removes an unrelated temporary directory
findings.evidence: clean at cli-packer/packer.py:78-83 accepts a `target` argument and never uses it -- line 83 is literally `_ = target`. What it actually does is create a fresh mkdtemp directory, create an empty `inner` subdirectory in it, and rmtree that new directory. The working directory the caller asked to clear, and the CACHE directory where stage() and write_token() leave staged bundles and the publishing token, are never touched. This is the same defect shape as intake-portal's expired() and verify_partner_signature(): a control that reports success while performing no work on its argument.
findings.impact: Callers believe post-build cleanup happened. Staged bundles and the persisted publishing token remain in /tmp/packer-cache indefinitely, extending the window in which the world-readable token from write_token is available to any local user, and leaving build artifacts on shared build hosts.
findings.recommendation: Remove the staged artifacts and the cached token for the given target, or delete the function so callers cannot rely on a cleanup that does not occur.

findings.title: Helper binaries resolved from PATH in a tool documented to run under sudo
findings.evidence: sign (cli-packer/packer.py:45) and publish (line 56) invoke bare executable names -- "gpg" and "uploader" -- via subprocess.run. The argument vectors are lists and no shell is involved, so there is no argument-injection issue; the exposure is the name resolution. A bare name is resolved against the inherited PATH at exec time. The README states the tool is documented as running under sudo for the publish command, and sudo configurations that do not set secure_path (or that use env_keep) preserve the caller's PATH. "uploader" in particular is not a standard system binary, so it is likely to be found in a user-writable directory.  Related locations: cli-packer/packer.py:45.
findings.impact: A local user who can prepend a directory to the PATH used by the sudo invocation, or who can write to any directory already on it, executes their own `uploader` (or `gpg`) as root, and additionally controls what is presented as a signed artifact.
findings.recommendation: Invoke the helpers by absolute path, or resolve them once against a fixed trusted directory list and pass an explicit env with a sanitized PATH. Ensure the documented sudo rule sets secure_path.
